title: Magnetic Field Strength: Force on a Moving Charge in a Magnetic Field
lead: Every force you have met so far points along a line you can draw on the page. This one does not. A magnetic field pushes a charge only while the charge is moving, and it pushes sideways, at right angles to the plane made by the velocity and the field. This section gives the size of that force as $\kF = \kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta$, turns the same relation round to say what the strength of a magnetic field is, derives the tesla and the gauss from that definition, and states right hand rule 1, which settles the direction.
objectives: Describe the effects of magnetic fields on moving charges.
Use the right hand rule 1 to determine the velocity of a charge, the direction of the magnetic field, and the direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge.
Calculate the magnetic force on a moving charge.
summary_html:
• Magnetic fields exert a force on a moving charge q, the magnitude of which is $\kF = \kq\kv\kBmag\sin\theta,$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of $\kv$ and $\kBmag$.
  • The SI unit for magnetic field strength $\kBmag$ is the tesla (T), which is related to other units by $1\;\text{T} = \frac{1\;\text{N}}{\text{C}\cdot\text{m/s}} = \frac{1\;\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}.$
  • The direction of the force on a moving charge is given by right hand rule 1 (RHR-1): Point the thumb of the right hand in the direction of $\kv$, the fingers in the direction of $\kBmag$, and a perpendicular to the palm points in the direction of $\kF$.
  • The force is perpendicular to the plane formed by $\kv$ and $\kBmag$. Since the force is zero if $\kv$ is parallel to $\kBmag$, charged particles often follow magnetic field lines rather than cross them.

figures.original_caption: Magnetic fields exert forces on moving charges. This force is one of the most basic known. The direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to the plane formed by v and B and follows right hand rule–1 (RHR-1) as shown. The magnitude of the force is proportional to q, v, B, and the sine of the angle between v and B.

exercises.prompt: A proton moves in the $-x$-direction and encounters a uniform magnetic field pointing in the $+x$-direction. In what direction is the resulting magnetic force on the proton?

options: The proton experiences no magnetic force.
answer.hint: The angle between the velocity and the field is 180°, and the force carries a factor of the sine of that angle.

exercises.prompt: A proton moves with a speed of 240 m/s in the $+x$-direction into a region of a 4.5-T uniform magnetic field directed 62° above the $+x$-direction in the $x,y$-plane. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on the proton.

answer.solution: The charge on a proton is $1.60\times 10^{-19}\;\text{C}$, and the angle between the velocity and the field is the 62° the question gives, so the magnitude follows from $F = qvB\sin\theta$ directly: $F = (1.60\times 10^{-19}\;\text{C})(240\;\text{m/s})(4.5\;\text{T})\sin 62^\circ$, which comes to about $1.5\times 10^{-16}\;\text{N}$. Note that only the angle between the two directions enters, not the plane they lie in\; the plane settles which way the force points, and right hand rule 1 puts that force out of the $x,y$-plane.

exercises.prompt: If a charged particle moves in a straight line through some region of space, can you say that the magnetic field in that region is necessarily zero?

answer.solution: No. The magnetic force carries a factor of $\sin\theta$, so it vanishes whenever the particle travels along the field lines, and a particle moving parallel or antiparallel to a strong field goes straight through it undeflected. A straight path is also possible when a magnetic force is present but is balanced by another force, as it is in the velocity selector the book meets later, where an electric force cancels the magnetic one. All that a straight path shows is that the net force on the particle is zero along its path, and there are several arrangements of field and particle that make it so.

exercises.prompt: What is the maximum magnitude of the force on an aluminum rod with a $0.100\text{-}\mu\text{C}$ charge that you pass between the poles of a 1.50-T permanent magnet at a speed of 5.00 m/s? In what direction is the force?

answer.hint: The force is greatest when the sine is one, which is when the rod crosses the field at right angles.
answer.solution: $7.50\times 10^{-7}\;\text{N}$ perpendicular to both the magnetic field lines and the velocity

exercises.prompt: (a) A cosmic ray proton moving toward the Earth at $5.00\times 10^{7}\;\text{m/s}$ experiences a magnetic force of $1.70\times 10^{-16}\;\text{N}$. What is the strength of the magnetic field if there is a $45^\circ$ angle between it and the proton’s velocity? (b) Is the value obtained in part (a) consistent with the known strength of the Earth’s magnetic field on its surface? Discuss.

answer.hint: This is the definition of the field strength used as it stands: divide the force by the charge, the speed and the sine of the angle.
answer.solution: (a) $3.01\times 10^{-5}\;\text{T}$ (b) This is slightly less then the magnetic field strength of $5\times 10^{-5}\;\text{T}$ at the surface of the Earth, so it is consistent.

exercises.prompt: (a) A physicist performing a sensitive measurement wants to limit the magnetic force on a moving charge in her equipment to less than $1.00\times 10^{-12}\;\text{N}$. What is the greatest the charge can be if it moves at a maximum speed of 30.0 m/s in the Earth’s field? (b) Discuss whether it would be difficult to limit the charge to less than the value found in (a) by comparing it with typical static electricity and noting that static is often absent.

answer.hint: Take the worst case, in which the charge crosses the field at right angles so the sine is one, and solve the force law for the charge.
answer.solution: (a) $6.67\times 10^{-10}\;\text{C}$ (taking the Earth’s field to be $5.00\times 10^{-5}\;\text{T}$) (b) Less than typical static, therefore difficult
